title: The Prismatic System
description: The Prismatic System is a compact formal symbolic language built from four layers: elements, binding, folding, and chains. Each layer introduces new rules that depend on everything before it, making it an excellent test of logical reasoning and step-by-step problem solving.
studyNote: This course was used in the original Coast learning study. Work through the four layers in order; each section maps directly to one lecture.

highlights.label: Layer 1 · Elements
highlights.desc: Three element types and the value rules that govern them

highlights.label: Layer 2 · Binding
highlights.desc: The binding operation (⊕) and its six type-and-order rules

highlights.label: Layer 3 · Folding
highlights.desc: The folding operation (∆) and conditional transformation rules

highlights.label: Layer 4 · Chains
highlights.desc: Multi-step sequences that combine every rule you've learned

title: The Science of Cooking
description: A four-lecture deep dive into the chemistry and physics behind everyday cooking, from the Maillard reaction and emulsification to gluten networks and the thermodynamics of bread rising. Inspired by Harvard's Science and Cooking curriculum.
studyNote: Work through the four lectures in order. Each section covers one lecture and its interactive kitchen diagnostics.

highlights.label: Lecture 1 · Maillard Reaction
highlights.desc: Non-enzymatic browning, flavor synthesis, and thermal kinetics

highlights.label: Lecture 2 · Emulsification
highlights.desc: Surfactants, interfacial tension, and stable emulsions

highlights.label: Lecture 3 · Gluten Network
highlights.desc: Gliadin, glutenin, and the viscoelastic dough matrix

highlights.label: Lecture 4 · Leavening
highlights.desc: Fermentation, gas laws, and why bread rises

title: The Memory Palace
description: Before paper, before printing, before phones, the people who built our civilisations held entire libraries in their heads. They were not smarter than you. They had a technique, and they treated memory as a craft. This lesson is that craft, rebuilt for one evening of your time.
studyNote: Work through the five sections in order. You will build and walk your own palace before the lesson ends.

highlights.label: Module 1 · Simonides
highlights.desc: The 477 BC banquet story that invented the method of loci

highlights.label: Modules 4–5 · Build & Encode
highlights.desc: Choose your route and learn the absurd, sensory encoding rules

highlights.label: Modules 6–7 · Practice
highlights.desc: Place ten items and walk your palace until recall is effortless

highlights.label: Module 9 · Real Studying
highlights.desc: Apply the palace to vocabulary, formulas, speeches, and exams

title: First-Principles Thinking
description: Most people reason by analogy: they copy what worked before and hope it works again. The few who break problems apart until only facts remain see what everyone else missed. That habit has a name, and it is older than any startup pitch deck. This lesson teaches you to reach for it on purpose.
studyNote: Work through the four sections in order. Each builds a step of the method, ending with problems you bring from your own studies.

highlights.label: Section 1 · The Habit
highlights.desc: Analogy vs first principles, and why defaults hide bad assumptions

highlights.label: Section 2 · Strip to Facts
highlights.desc: Separate what you know, what you assume, and what you are guessing

highlights.label: Section 3 · Rebuild
highlights.desc: Construct answers from verified pieces instead of inherited templates

highlights.label: Section 4 · Under Pressure
highlights.desc: Apply the method to exam questions, essays, and open-ended problems

title: The Polya Method
description: When students at Stanford were stuck on a problem, George Polya did not give them the answer. He gave them four questions to ask in order, until the answer assembled itself. Mathematicians have used his method for eighty years. This lesson is that sequence, rebuilt so you can run it on any problem you face.
studyNote: Work through the four phases in order: understand, plan, execute, and look back. Pedro will walk you through each stage with practice problems.

highlights.label: Phase 1 · Understand
highlights.desc: Restate the problem, identify unknowns, and check you really grasp the goal

highlights.label: Phase 2 · Plan
highlights.desc: Connect the problem to tools you know and choose a strategy before calculating

highlights.label: Phase 3 · Execute
highlights.desc: Carry out the plan step by step and track whether each step still makes sense

highlights.label: Phase 4 · Look Back
highlights.desc: Verify the result, reflect on the method, and generalize what you learned
